content:
The [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. RSD as a percentage — how spread out your numbers are relative to their mean. Enter your numbers (comma or space separated) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

The relative standard deviation (RSD) — also called the coefficient of variation — measures how spread out a set of numbers is relative to their average, as a percentage. A standard deviation of 5 means something very different for numbers around 10 than for numbers around 1,000, and the RSD fixes that by dividing the standard deviation by the mean. Scientists use it to compare the precision of measurements made on different scales, and analysts use it to compare the volatility of investments with very different prices.

## How to use the Relative Standard Deviation Calculator

Start by typing or pasting your numbers (comma or space separated). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Paste or type your numbers, separated by commas, spaces or line breaks.
2. Read the mean, the sample standard deviation and the RSD as a percentage.
3. Compare RSDs across different data sets — unlike the standard deviation, they are directly comparable.

## Formula

RSD = (sample standard deviation ÷ |mean|) × 100%. The sample standard deviation uses n − 1 in the denominator. The coefficient of variation is the same ratio without the × 100.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. For 4, 8, 15, 16, 23 and 42 the mean is 18 and the sample standard deviation is 13.49, so the RSD is 13.49 ÷ 18 × 100% = 74.95% — a very spread-out set. For 98, 100, 101, 102 and 99 the RSD is only about 1.58%. Try the same figures in the [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Numbers (comma or space separated): 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42), the [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) returns Count: 6, Mean: 18, Standard deviation (sample): 13.49, Relative standard deviation (RSD): 74.95%, Coefficient of variation: 0.7495. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## What the RSD tells you

A low RSD (a few percent) means the numbers cluster tightly around the mean — a precise measurement or a stable process. A high RSD (tens of percent) means the spread is large relative to the size of the numbers. As a rough guide, lab measurements often aim for an RSD under 5%, while financial returns routinely show RSDs over 50% — the number only makes sense against what is normal for the kind of data you have.

## Sample vs population standard deviation

This calculator uses the sample standard deviation (dividing by n − 1), which is the right choice when your numbers are a sample of a larger set — almost always the case for measurements and experiments. If your numbers are the entire population, the population standard deviation (dividing by n) would be slightly smaller, and so would the RSD. The difference shrinks as the sample grows.

## When the RSD breaks down

The RSD is meaningless when the mean is close to zero, because dividing by a tiny mean inflates the percentage enormously — a mean of 0.01 with a standard deviation of 1 gives an RSD of 10,000%. It also behaves oddly for data that can be negative. In those cases, use the plain standard deviation instead.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Use the RSD to compare precision across different scales — that is what it is for.
- Below 5% is tight for lab work; above 30% is very spread out for most measurements.
- If the mean is near zero, the RSD is meaningless — use the standard deviation instead.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is relative standard deviation?

The standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage. It measures spread relative to the size of the numbers, so data sets on different scales can be compared directly. Try it with your own numbers in the [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between RSD and coefficient of variation?

None — they are the same number. The coefficient of variation is the ratio (a decimal, e.g. 0.75) and the RSD is that ratio as a percentage (75%). Try it with your own numbers in the [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is a good RSD value?

It depends on the field. In analytical chemistry, under 5% is usually wanted; in finance, 50% or more is normal. Judge it against what is typical for your kind of data, not against an absolute number. Try it with your own numbers in the [Relative Standard Deviation Calculator](/relative-standard-deviation-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
